questions.evidence:
The class collects paper that is blank on one side for rough drafts. At first, students put every partly used sheet into a shared tray. The pile grows quickly, and everyone celebrates the amount of paper they think they have saved.

When Bess takes a sheet, she notices a classmate's family phone number on the reverse side. Another sheet contains a draft letter with personal information. The teacher pauses the collection and asks the class to sort the sheets before placing them in a public tray.

They keep clean, nonpersonal practice pages for reuse. Sheets containing private details go back to their owners for appropriate disposal. The class adds a clear instruction above the tray and assigns two volunteers to check new additions each afternoon.

The amount of reusable paper is smaller than the original pile, but the system now serves its purpose more carefully. Bess writes that saving resources works best when the process also respects the people whose information may appear on them.

questions.prompt: Why is a smaller reusable pile still an improvement?
